NEW DELHI: Former Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina has formally sought a new passport and national identity card (NID), taking a step towards her planned return from India in December.The information comes from a Monday letter sent by Hasina’s lawyers to the acting high commissioner at Bangladesh's embassy in Delhi, Preeti Rahman, Reuters reported.Hasina's lawyers at London-based Matrix Chambers requested the issuance of fresh documents. They cited the reported cancellation of her existing passport and NID by Bangladesh's interim government and other authorities."In view of the reported revocation of her existing Bangladeshi passport and National Identity Card (NID) by the Interim Government and other authorities, I respectfully request that you take the necessary steps to issue a new Bangladeshi passport and National Identity Card for our client," the lawyers wrote.The letter urged the authorities to process the applications "expeditiously", citing Hasina's Bangladeshi nationality and the country's "obligations arising under international human rights instruments".However, Bangladesh denied Hasina’s request, stating that the country does not provide "passport to a terrorist"."She is a fugitive criminal. We have an active extradition treaty with India. We want her handed over," Bangladesh state minister for foreign affairs, Humaiun Kobir, told reporters."Should we treat her like an ordinary commercial traveller and tell her ​to come and visit her ​in-laws’ residence?" Kobir jibed.According to Reuters, the request is the clearest indication yet that Hasina is taking steps to act on her stated intention to return in December, more than two years after a deadly uprising forced her from power. Her return could reignite political and legal tensions as Bangladesh attempts to restore stability and her Awami League party remains banned.Hasina intends to return and surrender before a court. Her aides said on Monday that the date would be announced after the completion of various formalities.Last week, the exiled leader the Associated Press she would prefer dying in her own land, among her own people.“If death is my destiny, I would rather die on the soil of my own country, among my own people,” Hasina said.In November 2025, Bangladesh's war-crimes tribunal sentenced Hasina to death in absentia for ordering a crackdown on the student-led uprising. She has denied the charges, rejected the verdict and questioned the legitimacy of the trial.The crackdown killed hundreds of protesters and left thousands injured. According to United Nations data cited by the Associated Press, nearly 1,400 people were killed during the unrest.Bangladesh has repeatedly sought Hasina's extradition from India. New Delhi has said the request is being examined through legal channels.Hasina's Awami League was Bangladesh's largest political party before it was banned following her removal from office. Several of its leaders and members have since been jailed, while others have gone into self-imposed exile in India and elsewhere.Having served as Prime Minister for 20 years across multiple terms, Hasina retains support among sections of the population. Her return could deepen political divisions as the country continues to deal with the aftermath of the upheaval.It could also have implications for Bangladesh's strained relationship with India, which deteriorated sharply after New Delhi gave the former prime minister refuge.
Article Summary: Sheikh Hasina has formally sought a new passport and national identity card (NID) The request is reportedly the clearest indication yet that Hasina is taking steps to act on her stated intention to return in December. Bangladesh denied Hasina’s request, stating that the country does not provide "passport to a terrorist"

Article Title: Cape Verde votes in election that could deliver first woman president
Article Text:
File photo: People drive past presidential campaign billboards for Cape Verde’s president Jose Maria Neves and presidential candidate Joana Rosa in Praia, Cape Verde

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Cape Verde voted on Sunday in a presidential election that could see the island nation elect its first woman head of state since independence from Portugal in 1975.Incumbent Jose Maria Neves is seeking a second term against former justice minister Joana Rosa, whose campaign has focused on the need for political balance and better opportunities for young people.The election comes as the West African archipelago grapples with a steady exodus of young people seeking work abroad. With a population of around 500,000, Cape Verde has a larger diaspora overseas, particularly in the United States and Portugal.Nearly 77,000 Cape Verdeans living abroad are registered to vote, accounting for almost a fifth of the electorate.Neves, who served as prime minister for 15 years before becoming president in 2021, has pledged to build cross-party support to improve housing, healthcare and education, create jobs and raise wages. He has also promised to organise a youth summit during a second term.Rosa, the candidate of the opposition Movement for Democracy (MpD), has called for policies that allow young people to build their futures at home rather than leave the country. She has campaigned around the idea that young people should "build their ⁠futures here at home and prevent the continued exodus of young Cape Verdeans abroad”. She has also made the need for a balance of power central to her campaign.Neves belongs to the African Party for the Independence of Cape Verde (PAICV), which won a majority in May's parliamentary election, securing 37 of the 72 seats and ending a decade of MpD-led government. A Rosa victory would place the presidency and government in opposing political camps.Rosa is the first woman to contest the presidency since Cape Verde gained independence in 1975. While women have held senior cabinet positions, the country has never had a woman president or prime minister.Under Cape Verde's parliamentary-presidential system, the prime minister holds most executive authority, while the president has veto powers and a mediating role.Polling stations were scheduled to open at 8 am and close at 6 pm local time. Provisional results were expected within two or three days. If no candidate secures more than 50% of the vote, the two leading candidates will face each other in a runoff on November 29.
Article Summary: Incumbent Jose Maria Neves is seeking a second term against former justice minister Joana Rosa. The election comes as the West African archipelago grapples with a steady exodus of young people seeking work abroad. With a population of around 500,000, Cape Verde has a larger diaspora overseas.

Article Title: Fifth soldier dies after grass fire sweeps through Canadian military base during training exercise
Article Text:
Pvt William Douglas Dal Bianco died on Friday at a hospital in Ontario.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A fifth Canadian soldier has died from injuries sustained when a fast-spreading grass fire swept through a military training exercise in Alberta last month, the Canadian Armed Forces said on Saturday.Pvt William Douglas Dal Bianco died on Friday at a hospital in Ontario, where he had been receiving treatment since the October 17 incident at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, southeast of Edmonton.Four soldiers were killed earlier in the incident, while 24 others remain hospitalised, according to the Canadian Armed Forces.The fire broke out as troops from the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, were conducting a live-fire training exercise. Strong winds caused the flames to spread rapidly towards the soldiers, catching several of them off guard.According to the BBC, 38 military personnel were injured in the incident, with 14 having been discharged from hospital by Saturday.Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney expressed condolences over Dal Bianco’s death, saying the soldier and his colleagues had been training to defend the country."With their bright futures still before them, they chose to safeguard ours.That is service," Carney said in a social media post.The four soldiers killed earlier were Pvt Shaun Farrell, 23, from Prince Albert, Saskatchewan; Pvt Aidan Goulding, 23, from North Vancouver, British Columbia; Pvt Hayden Lykkemark, 19, from Langley, British Columbia; and Sgt Morgan Wong, 26, from Edmonton.The BBC reported that an initial investigation indicated the fire was likely sparked by a grenade launcher being fired at the base's grenade range. Firefighters stationed at the base were aware of the blaze but could not immediately tackle it because the area was considered dangerous due to the possibility of unexploded ammunition.The fire reportedly spread across a kilometre within seconds, prompting an overnight firefighting operation as nearby hospitals received large numbers of injured personnel.Military police are investigating the incident, while a separate military board of inquiry will examine the circumstances surrounding the tragedy and recommend measures to prevent similar accidents.Carney had earlier described the incident as one of the worst peacetime tragedies involving Canada's armed forces on Canadian soil.
Article Summary: Pvt William Douglas Dal Bianco died on Friday at a hospital in Ontario. He had been receiving treatment since the October 17 incident at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, southeast of Edmonton. Four soldiers were killed earlier in the incident, while 24 others remain hospitalised.

Article Title: Spain’s Canary Islands record highest daily migrant arrivals since 2020; 1,488 rescued
Article Text:
1,488 migrants rescued in a single day as arrivals to Spain’s Canary Islands hit a six-year high/Image: Reuters

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Spain’s Canary Islands recorded their highest number of migrant arrivals in a single day since 2020 after 1,488 people were rescued from 14 boats on Saturday, as the Atlantic migration route from West Africa saw a fresh increase in crossings, EFE news agency reported, citing the maritime rescue service.The latest arrivals surpassed the previous daily record of 1,461 people rescued in waters near the archipelago on November 7, 2020, according to maritime rescue authorities.The increase follows a rise in arrivals from West African countries since October, placing additional pressure on reception and emergency services on some islands. Smaller and less densely populated islands have been particularly affected.El Hierro, one of the smallest islands in the archipelago, received 12 of the 14 boats on Saturday. The remaining two arrived in Gran Canaria and Tenerife.One of the boats carried 240 people, including 12 women and 36 children. Authorities said those rescued were taken to El Hierro, with most coming from Senegal, Gambia and Guinea-Conakry.Spain’s Territorial Policy Minister Angel Victor Torres is scheduled to visit El Hierro on Sunday to discuss the increase in migrant arrivals.The Atlantic crossing from West Africa to the Canary Islands remains one of the world’s deadliest migration routes. Thousands of people attempt the journey each year in overcrowded boats, risking rough seas, strong currents and long distances in an effort to reach Spanish territory.Crossings typically increase during autumn, when sea conditions are generally calmer and more favourable for travel.Despite the latest surge, overall arrivals to the Canary Islands remain lower than last year. Government figures show that the number of migrants reaching the archipelago between January and October 31 was down 5.5% compared with the same period in the previous year.
Article Summary: 1,488 people were rescued from 14 boats on Saturday. The latest arrivals surpassed the previous daily record of 1,461 people rescued in waters near the archipelago on November 7, 2020. The increase follows a rise in arrivals from West African countries since October.

Article Title: Philippines-China tensions: Key events that have deepened South China Sea rift
Article Text:
Philippines president Ferdinand Marcos Jr

2025: Maritime confrontations and growing military cooperation

2026: Military drills, diplomatic disputes and fresh clashes

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Relations between the Philippines and China have deteriorated under Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr, with Manila pivoting back towards the United States, which supports the Southeast Asian nation in its maritime disputes with Beijing.A series of confrontations involving coast guard vessels, naval ships and aircraft, alongside military exercises and diplomatic exchanges, has escalated tensions between the two countries. Here is a timeline of key developments during 2025 and 2026, as per Reuters news agency.In January, the Philippines deployed ships and aircraft to monitor China's largest coast guard vessel in its exclusive economic zone. The next month, Manila accused the Chinese navy of conducting a dangerous flyby near Scarborough Shoal, an allegation disputed by Beijing. In March, satellite images showed China deploying two H-6 bombers around the disputed shoal.In May, the Philippines challenged a Chinese research vessel over what it described as an illegal marine survey off the coast of Ilocos.In August, the Philippine and Indian navies sailed together in the South China Sea for the first time.Tensions also escalated around Scarborough Shoal, with Manila criticising what it called dangerous manoeuvres by Chinese vessels and saying they had led to a collision involving a Chinese ship. China separately claimed it had driven away a US destroyer that sailed near the shoal, while the US Navy said its operation was in accordance with international law.In September 2025, China approved the creation of a national nature reserve at Scarborough Shoal. Later that month, the Chinese coast guard fired water cannon at Philippine ships near the shoal. Manila described the action as aggressive and said one person had been injured.In October, the Philippines accused the Chinese coast guard of ramming and firing water cannon at its fisheries vessels near Thitu Island, which is occupied by the Philippines.In January, China said it had driven away Philippine aircraft that had illegally entered the airspace over Scarborough Shoal. Later that month, the Philippine and US militaries conducted joint exercises near the disputed feature.In February, the Philippines joined maritime drills with the United States and Japan in the South China Sea, while China also conducted exercises in the disputed waters.In March, the Philippines apprehended Filipino nationals suspected of spying for China. China subsequently said it had expelled two Philippine aircraft over Scarborough Shoal. Manila also accused a Chinese navy vessel of directing its fire-control radar at one of its ships. Later in the month, China conducted naval, air and coast guard patrols around the shoal, following the resumption of talks between Beijing and Manila on energy cooperation.In April, the Philippine Coast Guard accused Chinese forces of directly firing flares at one of its aircraft in the South China Sea. China later held live-fire drills in waters near Luzon as Manila and Washington staged military exercises. The Philippines and the US also conducted drills in Palawan province, near the South China Sea. As part of their war games, the two countries deployed an anti-ship missile system in a province near Taiwan.In May, Manila said a Chinese vessel had conducted illegal research near the Reed Bank, an area in the South China Sea believed to be rich in gas resources.In June, the Philippines took diplomatic action against China over a floating structure in the South China Sea. Beijing subsequently announced sanctions against Philippine Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro, accusing him of having "repeatedly made erroneous remarks concerning China."In July, the Philippines accused Chinese coast guard personnel of striking a Philippine navy sailor on the head with a wooden baton during an encounter in the South China Sea. Manila also said a Chinese coast guard vessel had fired water cannon at a Philippine government fisheries vessel near Scarborough Shoal.In September, the Philippines accused the Chinese coast guard of ramming one of its boats during a refuelling mission. Manila also alleged that China had obstructed a resupply mission to its troops stationed at Second Thomas Shoal.In October, the Philippines criticised China's ambassador over what it described as a "thinly veiled threat" of force. Manila later said it had summoned the ambassador over remarks it considered threatening.Against this backdrop, Southeast Asian leaders gathered in Manila on Sunday for the 49th Asean Summit, the final summit of the Philippines’ year as bloc chair. US President Donald Trump is among the world leaders due to attend, and a special US-Asean meeting is planned for November 17.Chinese Premier Li Qiang is also expected to attend, though President Xi Jinping is not. The South China Sea is high on the agenda, but hopes for a breakthrough have faded. Three regional diplomats said China and Asean have reportedly made progress on a Code of Conduct but will not be able to conclude the decades-long negotiations this year, as had been agreed.
Article Summary: Relations between the Philippines and China have deteriorated under Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. Manila pivoting back towards the United States, which supports the Southeast Asian nation in its maritime disputes with Beijing. A series of confrontations involving coast guard vessels, naval ships and aircraft, alongside military exercises and diplomatic exchanges has escalated tensions.

Article Title: 80 years after genocide convention, Myanmar faces historic ICJ verdict
Article Text:
Why the Myanmar ruling matters for Israel's Gaza case

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Nearly eight decades after the world adopted the genocide convention in the aftermath of the Holocaust, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) is approaching a historic moment.On November 19, the world's highest court will deliver a landmark ruling on whether Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya Muslim minority. The verdict could shape the future interpretation of international law and have significant implications for South Africa's separate genocide case against Israel over the war in Gaza.According to The Guardian, the ruling could establish an important legal benchmark for determining how states are held responsible for genocide, particularly how courts assess the intent to destroy an ethnic, religious, racial or national group.The case was brought by The Gambia against Myanmar in November 2019 under the 1948 Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide. The Gambia accused Myanmar's military of carrying out a campaign of violence against the Rohingya population in Rakhine state, particularly during the 2017 crackdown.According to the UN refugee agency UNHCR, around 700,000 Rohingya fled to neighbouring Bangladesh following the military operations that began on August 25, 2017.In January 2020, the ICJ ordered Myanmar to take all measures within its power to prevent acts prohibited under the Genocide Convention against the Rohingya and preserve evidence relating to the allegations.The court rejected Myanmar's preliminary objections in July 2022, ruling that it had jurisdiction to hear the case.Public hearings on the merits took place from January 12 to 29, 2026, with the court now preparing to deliver its final judgment.The November 19 judgment could mark a first in the history of the ICJ. Although the court has previously recognised that genocide occurred in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, it has never directly held a state responsible for committing genocide. A ruling against Myanmar would therefore be a landmark in the enforcement of the Genocide Convention and the international legal accountability of states.The judgment will also be closely watched for its potential implications for South Africa's genocide case against Israel over its military campaign in Gaza.South Africa filed the case at the ICJ in December 2023, accusing Israel of violating the 1948 Genocide Convention through its military operations in the Palestinian territory. Israel has rejected the allegations, maintaining that its war is directed against Hamas and not the Palestinian population.The two cases are legally separate, but both require the ICJ to examine whether the evidence establishes the specific intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a protected national, ethnic, racial or religious group.The Myanmar judgment could provide important guidance on how the court assesses genocidal intent, particularly when examining patterns of military conduct, civilian killings, destruction of settlements and statements by political and military leaders.The timing is also important. The Gaza case remains at the written pleadings stage. In May 2026, the ICJ set November 22, 2027, as the deadline for South Africa to submit its reply to Israel's counter-memorial.Israel will then have until May 22, 2029, to file its rejoinder. This means the Myanmar judgment could offer legal guidance while the proceedings against Israel are still underway.The Guardian also highlighted the political implications of the ruling, particularly for the United States, which has strongly backed Israel.US ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz warned that the ICJ must not establish a genocide standard that could be applied against allied soldiers. The concern reflects the wider international debate over how the Genocide Convention should be interpreted and applied to military operations.
Article Summary: The International Court of Justice (ICJ) will deliver a landmark ruling on whether Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya Muslim minority. The verdict could shape the future interpretation of international law. It could also have significant implications for South Africa's separate genocide case against Israel over the war in Gaza.
